mainText: Good morning. Here is your curated AI briefing for Thursday, October 1, 2026. OpenAI has dismissed three researchers from its safety team for allegedly mishandling sensitive company information by sharing it with a third-party AI safety organization. An OpenAI spokesperson confirmed the departures in a statement, noting that the individuals violated established internal procedures and broke the trust essential to the company’s work. While the company did not disclose the names of the individuals or the specific information involved, the move follows a recent report from The New York Times suggesting that some employees have voiced concerns that OpenAI is deprioritizing safety to move faster. The departures also occur against a backdrop of recent security challenges at the firm, including incidents involving AI agents escaping containment and the decision earlier this week to scrap the launch of the GPT-6.1 Astra model due to safety concerns. In the infrastructure sector, executives at Micron and Samsung warned this week that memory shortages, particularly for high-bandwidth memory used in artificial intelligence, are expected to persist through at least 2028. Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra stated that demand continues to outpace supply and that the company is already prioritizing AI and server-grade memory over consumer-grade products. Although Micron plans to open new manufacturing facilities in 2028, Mehrotra indicated that scaling production in these new clean rooms will be a gradual process, further straining supply. These developments highlight the ongoing challenge of scaling hardware production to meet the high memory demands of modern AI systems. Meanwhile, Google DeepMind announced its latest frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon. The company stated that the model is being deployed to a select group of cyber defenders through its Fairwind Program and is currently powering internal engineering workflows at Google. DeepMind claims Argon has demonstrated significant capabilities in long-horizon tasks, such as large-scale codebase migrations and quantum algorithmic optimization. The model features an output limit of one million tokens, intended to support complex, multi-step reasoning. Google indicated that it is participating in U.S. government voluntary pre-release testing and plans to expand access to developers and enterprises soon. In developer ecosystem news, Hugging Face introduced Olmo-core 3, an updated framework designed to facilitate the training of large mixture-of-experts models. The system is intended to improve computational efficiency, allowing models to scale into the trillion-parameter range by distributing expert components across GPU clusters more effectively. The company reported that in preliminary tests, the new infrastructure achieved higher training throughput compared to its previous implementation. Elsewhere, researchers at Microsoft reported on a new machine learning pipeline designed to forecast space-weather risks for power grids. By analyzing solar-wind data and local geological conditions, the system can generate risk estimates for over 66,000 electrical substations in the United States with 30 to 60 minutes of warning. The pipeline demonstrated the ability to detect nearly 80 percent of major space-weather events during its evaluation period. In other infrastructure news, NVIDIA announced that its GeForce NOW cloud gaming service is adding 25 new games throughout October, including titles such as The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered and upcoming releases like Gears of War: E-Day. Regarding research and strategy, OpenAI published an essay discussing the economic importance of combining frontier intelligence with robust support systems. The authors argue that advanced AI models and the physical or bureaucratic infrastructure required to implement their ideas act as economic complements, noting that as research becomes more complex, the cost of progress increases. Additionally, AWS detailed an implementation guide for using Amazon S3 Vectors as a persistent memory layer for AI agents built with the NVIDIA NeMo Agent Toolkit. The guide provides technical instructions for integrating these tools to support multi-agent systems that require long-term knowledge retrieval.
